name: Acute Bacterial Prostatitis

possible: Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis (younger sexually active men — different management)
pathogens.why: Acute bacterial prostatitis in older men typically reflects the same uropathogens as other UTIs, ascending into the prostate; in younger sexually active men, sexually transmitted pathogens should specifically be considered as they require different antibiotic coverage and partner management.

investigations.why: Identifies the causative organism; this is preferred over prostatic secretion sampling in the acute setting given bacteremia risk with prostatic massage.
Bacteremia is not uncommon in acute prostatitis and positive cultures help confirm the organism.

investigations.test: Post-void residual / bladder scan (if retention suspected)
investigations.why: Urinary retention is a recognized complication requiring catheterization (suprapubic preferred over urethral if prostatitis is causing obstruction).

investigations.test: STI testing (NAAT for gonorrhea/chlamydia) if risk factors present
investigations.why: Identifies sexually transmitted causes requiring different management and partner notification.

reason: in a male patient is consistent with acute bacterial prostatitis. Antibiotics with reliable prostatic tissue penetration are required, and digital rectal examination should be performed gently (vigorous prostatic massage is avoided in the acute setting due to bacteremia risk).

clinicalPearls: Acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP) typically presents as a severe illness with dysuria, urinary frequency, and pain in the prostatic, pelvic, or perineal region, and may be accompanied by fever, rigors, and/or bladder outlet obstruction (Harrison 22e p.1089).

The prostate is involved in the majority of febrile UTI cases in men; ABP should be specifically suspected when a man presents with UTI plus systemic symptoms but no other clear anatomic source such as pyelonephritis (Harrison 22e p.1089, p.1136).

Bacteriuria documented on urine culture is what distinguishes the less common bacterial prostatitis syndromes (acute and chronic) from the far more common chronic pelvic pain syndrome, which is NOT associated with bacteriuria and is NOT improved by antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Men with febrile UTI may show an elevated serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) and an enlarged prostate and seminal vesicles on ultrasound, supporting prostatic involvement; PSA is therefore not interpretable as a cancer marker during acute infection (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Prostatitis is largely unrepresented in UTI clinical trial data, so complicated-UTI practice guidelines cannot be assumed to apply to prostatitis; older literature suggests prolonged therapy with prostate-penetrating agents may be needed (Harrison 22e p.1087).
harrison.pathophysiology: Prostatitis can complicate ascending cystitis or arise hematogenously, for example as a metastatic focus of Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia. Infectious prostatitis is almost always bacterial and is far less common than the noninfectious chronic pelvic pain syndrome. In general, most genitourinary infections in men ascend from the urethra to the bladder, with the prostate becoming involved as part of febrile UTI; less than 2% of UTIs are hematogenous, usually from virulent organisms such as S. aureus and Salmonella. Obstruction from prostatic hypertrophy after age 50 promotes urinary stasis and is a major reason UTI incidence in older men approaches that in women (Harrison 22e p.1087, p.1089, p.1131).
additionalDifferentials: Chronic bacterial prostatitis (CBP) — presents insidiously as recurrent episodes of cystitis, sometimes with pelvic and perineal pain, usually without systemic signs of infection; should be suspected with recurrent UTI not in the context of catheterization (Harrison 22e p.1089, p.1136).
Pyelonephritis — another febrile genitourinary infection that must be excluded as the anatomic source before attributing systemic symptoms to ABP (Harrison 22e p.1136).
Acute cystitis in men — uncommon and warrants caution; urine culture should be obtained in all male UTI to help identify a prostatic focus (Harrison 22e p.1089).
infectionMimics: Pyelonephritis — overlapping febrile UTI presentation; distinguished by flank/costovertebral angle pain and an upper-tract source (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Urethritis — urethral pain, pruritus, or discharge should prompt evaluation for sexually transmitted infections (Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium) rather than assuming prostatitis (Harrison 22e p.1087).
nonInfectiousMimics: Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (formerly chronic prostatitis) — a noninfectious disorder that is the far more common cause of prostatic-type symptoms, with NO bacteriuria and NO response to antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.1089).
Benign prostatic hypertrophy with obstructive uropathy / urinary retention — can produce lower urinary tract symptoms and predispose to UTI (Harrison 22e p.1089, p.1131).
additionalInvestigations: Urine culture in all male UTI — documenting bacteriuria differentiates bacterial prostatitis from chronic pelvic pain syndrome; dipstick and/or microscopy alone are not sufficient (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Cross-sectional imaging (CT or ultrasound) for men with febrile UTI, including the first episode, if not previously done, to evaluate for urinary tract abnormalities or obstruction (Harrison 22e p.1089).
Evaluation for urinary retention / prostatic focus in men with recurrent cystitis (Harrison 22e p.1089).
Urologic consultation referral if the diagnosis of UTI is unclear or UTI is recurrent (Harrison 22e p.1089).
redFlags: Bladder outlet obstruction or urinary retention accompanying ABP (Harrison 22e p.1089).
Fever and rigors indicating a severe, systemic illness (Harrison 22e p.1089).
Identification of a prostatic abscess — should prompt urologic specialist consultation (Harrison 22e p.1136).
Symptoms predictive of surgically correctable disease in men with febrile UTI: urinary retention, early UTI recurrence, hematuria at follow-up, and voiding difficulties (Harrison 22e p.1089).
harrison.prognosis: ABP is typically a severe acute illness but is amenable to therapy with prostate-penetrating antimicrobials. A prostatic abscess is a recognized complication requiring urologic intervention. Chronic bacterial prostatitis recurrences are not uncommon. Men with febrile UTI and none of the warning features (retention, early recurrence, hematuria, voiding difficulty) generally have normal upper and lower urinary tracts on urologic workup, implying a favorable structural prognosis (Harrison 22e p.1089, p.1136).
pitfalls: Do not attribute prostatic-type symptoms to bacterial prostatitis without bacteriuria; absence of bacteriuria points to chronic pelvic pain syndrome, which will not respond to antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.1089).
Do not interpret an elevated PSA during febrile male UTI as a cancer marker — acute prostatic infection itself raises PSA and prostate/seminal vesicle size on imaging (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Do not assume complicated-UTI guideline regimens and durations apply to prostatitis, since prostatitis is largely absent from UTI trial data and may require prolonged prostate-penetrating therapy (Harrison 22e p.1087).
Do not overlook a prostatic focus or urinary retention in men presenting with recurrent cystitis (Harrison 22e p.1089).
harrison.severityClassification: Prostatitis is categorized as acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP) versus chronic bacterial prostatitis (CBP). ABP is a typically severe illness with systemic features (fever, rigors, possible bladder outlet obstruction); CBP presents insidiously as recurrent cystitis with pelvic/perineal pain and typically without systemic signs, often managed in the ambulatory setting. Both are distinct from noninfectious chronic pelvic pain syndrome (Harrison 22e p.1089, p.1136).
